proof: Retro Porting Toolkit helps old games become native apps. The game logic stays the game logic. The hardware around it becomes a modern runtime, so ports can add things the original console could not.
philosophy: Run native. A port can target Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, or the browser without shipping an emulator core as the main experience.
Open the view. Widescreen can show more of the game world instead of stretching the old picture.
Keep the original safe. Mods, translations, save states, and rewind layer on top of the game file you provide.
Use modern hardware. A phone gyro can stand in for a tilt cartridge. Local weather can stand in for a sunlight sensor.
Make work reusable. Better debug tools and release systems should help the next port, not only one game.
constraintsIntro: The best ports keep a faithful path underneath the enhancements. Turn the extra feature off and the original behavior should still be there.

stories.title: The screen was smaller than the world.
stories.body: Some games already keep more of the map in memory than the original screen could show. A careful widescreen mode can reveal that extra space while keeping the old 4:3 path intact.
stories.alt: Mega Man Zero running with the view opened past the original Game Boy Advance width

stories.title: Boktai still runs on sunlight. Yours.
stories.body: Boktai used a real light sensor in the cartridge. The recomp keeps that idea and maps it to modern inputs. Local weather can drive the sunlight gauge, while the original game file stays untouched.
stories.alt: Boktai running with its solar gauge driven by local weather

stories.title: Change the words while the game runs.
stories.body: Runtime text replacement lets a translator edit a line, reload it, and see the result in-game. It is useful for fan translation, accessibility, and quick iteration without patching the original file.
stories.alt: Faxanadu running as a native PC application
